interviewQuestions.question: What is pipelining, and does it make an individual instruction execute faster?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
⭐ **Q: What is pipelining, and does it make an individual instruction execute faster?**

I'd start by defining it as an overlap technique, not a speed-up-one-instruction technique. Pipelining splits instruction execution into stages built from separate hardware — fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back — so while one instruction is decoding, the next can already be fetching. Nothing shortens any single instruction's own journey through those stages; if anything, the pipeline registers between stages add a small fixed overhead.

What pipelining buys you is **throughput**: once the pipeline is full, a new instruction can finish nearly every cycle instead of every N cycles. I'd use the laundromat analogy — three machines running different loads at once finish more laundry per hour, but no single load washes and dries any faster.

**Testing:** whether you distinguish latency from throughput — a very common trip-up when people first meet pipelining.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Pipelining and instruction latency

interviewQuestions.question: For an N-stage pipeline, why is the achieved speedup always less than N?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
**Q: For an N-stage pipeline, why is the achieved speedup always less than N?**

Two reasons I'd cover. First, there's a fixed startup cost: filling the pipeline takes N-1 cycles before the first instruction fully completes, and this fill cost gets amortized over however many instructions run — for a short program it dominates and speedup stays well below N.

Second, and the bigger real-world factor, is hazards. Structural hazards (two instructions wanting the same hardware), data hazards (one instruction needs a result the previous one hasn't produced yet), and control hazards (branches whose target isn't known yet) all force stall cycles or bubbles, leaving stages idle instead of doing useful work. I'd close by noting that real CPUs spend a lot of design effort — forwarding, branch prediction, out-of-order execution — specifically clawing back this gap between ideal and real speedup.

**Testing:** whether you can name the concrete mechanisms (fill time, hazards) rather than just asserting "real life isn't ideal."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why ideal speedup isn't reached
